q: The technician opens the battery lockers of the catamaran and shows you this. What do you want to be sure of before he closes them?
a: That each engine has its own starter battery and the house bank is separate from both
o: That all five batteries are wired as one bank, for the most capacity
That the house bank starts the engines when the starter batteries are low
That the port engine battery also runs the fridge, being the strongest one
why: Separate banks: a flat house bank after a night at anchor still leaves each engine its own battery to start.

q: The technician shows you the battery switches and gives you this advice. How will you actually run them?
a: ENGINE and HOUSE on at sea and at anchor; BOTH only for a flat-battery start; all off leaving the boat
o: BOTH on all week, as he says, so the fridge and the lights can draw on both banks together
HOUSE off under way so the alternator puts the whole charge into the engine battery
ENGINE off at anchor so the fridge and the lights cannot flatten the starter battery
why: Both banks on keeps them separate; BOTH joins them, so a flat house bank takes the engine battery with it.

fig.title: Battery switches
lines: Technician: "just leave BOTH on all week"

q: First morning at anchor; you read the battery monitor before switching anything on. What state is the house bank in?
a: Full — a rested bank at 12.7 V is near 100 %
o: Half — 12.7 V is midway between flat and full
Flat — anything under 13 V needs the engine now
Overcharged — a bank at rest should read 12.0 V
why: Rested, no load: 12.7 V full, 12.4 V about 75 %, 12.2 V half, 12.0 V or less flat.

q: At check-in the technician points at the voltmeter and says the batteries are 'perfect'. What does this reading actually tell you?
a: Only that the charger is working — the state of the bank shows after a rest off the charger
o: That the bank is full and will hold 13.8 V all night at anchor
That the bank is being overcharged and the charger must go off now
That the batteries are new — an old bank never gets up to 13.8 V
why: On charge the charger sets the volts (13.8 float, 14.4 bulk); the bank's own voltage is read after an hour at rest.

q: You are going through the panel with the technician and see this. What do you do?
a: Note it on the form and ask the base to sort it before you sail — the charger is off or the bank is dead
o: Accept it — the bank will come up once you run the engine on Sunday morning
Switch to BOTH so the engine battery carries the house bank for the week
Move the cable to another pedestal socket, see the light come on and sign
why: Plugged in, the bank should read 13.8–14.4 V; 11.8 V with current going out means no charge — and ask how old the bank is.

q: The technician waves at the panel, says 'all the usual' and heads for the engine bay. What do you ask him to do first?
a: Switch on each breaker in turn and show you what it feeds
o: Leave every breaker on so you can find out as you go
Explain the 230 V side only — the 12 V side is obvious
Hand you the boat manual to read the panel on passage
why: You will be finding these at night in a blow; VHF, instruments and the windlass each have their own breaker.

q: Your crew asks whether the kettle and the hairdryer will work in the bays. What do you tell them?
a: Only on shore power — at anchor the 230 V outlets are dead and the inverter runs a laptop, not a kettle
o: Yes — flip the 230 V main breaker and the batteries feed the outlets directly
Yes with the engine running — the alternator powers the 230 V side of the panel
Yes — switch the charger on and it converts 12 V into 230 V for the outlets
why: The 230 V side is live only on shore power or a generator; a 300 W inverter will not run a 2 kW kettle.

fig.title: Main panel
lines: Right: 230 V AC — RCD, charger, outlets, water heater
Inverter 300 W: one socket at the chart table

q: The technician plugs the shore cable in and goes to fetch the inventory list. You look at the 230 V panel. What do you do?
a: Unplug it and tell the base — the pedestal is miswired; no 230 V until it is fixed
o: Press the RCD test button to clear the warning and carry on
Ignore it — polarity only matters on American 110 V boats
Turn the plug the other way round in the pedestal socket
why: Reverse polarity leaves the live side on breakers that should be neutral; an RCD does not make it safe.

q: Sunday 10:00, the technician has gone and you are ready to cast off from the pontoon. In what order do you deal with the shore power?
a: Charger and 230 V main off, pedestal switch off, unplug the pedestal end first, then the boat end, stow the cable
o: Unplug the boat end first, hand the live cable to a crew on the pontoon, then the pedestal end
Leave it plugged in until the engine is running for a last charge, then pull both ends at once
Pull both ends, leave the cable on the pontoon for the base to collect, cast off
why: Dead before you touch it, pedestal end first so no live plug lies on deck; the cable is on the inventory.

q: You ask the technician to start the engine and watch the battery monitor. What do you tell him?
a: It is not charging — the alternator or belt needs looking at before you leave
o: All good — volts must drop a little when the engine takes its load
All good — the alternator only starts charging above 2000 rpm
All good — it charges the engine battery, which is not on this monitor
why: With the engine running the monitor should show about 14 V and current going in; 12.3 V and −8 A is no charge.

q: The technician resets the breaker, the windlass runs, and he moves on. What rule do you take away, and what do you ask before he goes?
a: Engine running whenever you use it; and where the spare fuses are, for anything that blows instead of tripping
o: Breaker on all week so the remote always works; and whether the base will come out if it trips again
Use it with the engine off at anchor so the alternator is unloaded; and the make of the motor
Start the engine only if it stalls; and whether the house bank can be switched in to help it
why: The windlass draws 80–100 A; the alternator covers it and the engine is ready. A breaker resets, a fuse needs a spare.

fig.title: Windlass
lines: Breaker 80 A at the chart table
Tripped on the first test, reset

q: Evening in the bay, the fridge is the only thing running. Do you leave it on overnight?
a: Yes — about 5 A for 10 h is 50 Ah, a quarter of the bank; charge with the engine in the morning
o: No — switch it off at night; 5 A will flatten 200 Ah well before dawn
Yes, and the lights and the inverter too — 200 Ah is enough for the week
Only with BOTH selected so the engine battery shares the night's load
why: Amps × hours = amp-hours; a lead-acid bank should not go below half, so 50 Ah of 200 is fine.

q: Saturday night you switch on NAV LIGHTS and walk out along the pontoon to look at the bow. This is what you see. What do you do?
a: Note the dead starboard light on the form and ask the base to replace the bulb before you sail
o: Sail with the tricolour instead — it shows the same arcs
Buy a bulb in town on Monday and fit it yourself
Accept it — you plan to be in a harbour every night
why: Test the lights at the pontoon, at night, from outside; the base replaces what is dead.

fig.note: Pontoon, 21:00 — seen from ahead, NAV LIGHTS on

q: You switch on the ANCHOR breaker and look up from the pontoon. What have you confirmed?
a: The all-round white anchor light works — the one to show every night at anchor
o: The steaming light works — the one to show at anchor with the engine off
The tricolour works — show it at anchor to save the battery
The deck light works — enough for a quiet bay with no traffic
why: At anchor at night a vessel shows an all-round white light (Rule 30); test it where you can see it.

q: The technician reads this off the inventory list without opening the floor. How do you check it before you sign?
a: Switch to ON and hear it run, lift the float for AUTO, find the hand-pump handle
o: Trust the panel light — it only comes on if the pump is wired
Leave it on AUTO and look at the bilge again at check-out
Set it to OFF so it cannot drain the batteries at anchor
why: A pump that was never heard is a pump that may not run; AUTO stays selected all week.

fig.title: Bilge pump
lines: Electric: float switch in the bilge
Hand pump in the cockpit, handle in the locker

q: What do you do with these two before you sign, and what do you ask?
a: Press TEST on each and hear it; ask what to do when the gas alarm sounds
o: Take the battery out of the CO alarm so it does not chirp at night
Note that they are fitted — testing them trips the panel breaker
Ask for a spare detector in case this one goes off falsely
why: Gas alarm: close the bottle valve, no switches, ventilate; a dead CO alarm goes on the form.

fig.title: Alarms
lines: Gas detector: sensor in the bilge, panel at the galley
CO alarm in the saloon, 9 V battery

q: The technician says 'you will not need these' and skips them. What do you ask him to show you anyway?
a: The solar controller charging, and the generator started with water at its exhaust; note the hours
o: Nothing — extras you do not use are not your problem at check-out
The generator fuel level only; a solar panel has nothing to check
The panel wiring under the bimini, with the controller switched off
why: Anything on the inventory is yours for the week; a generator is checked like the engine — hours and raw water.

fig.title: Also fitted
lines: Solar 200 W on the bimini, controller at the chart table
Generator strainer under the aft bunk

q: The technician brings this cable to plug you in. What do you do?
a: Refuse it and ask for another — a damaged 230 V cable on a wet pontoon can kill
o: Tape over the cut and plug in — the RCD will trip if anything leaks
Use it with dry hands and keep the cut end on the boat, not the pontoon
Plug it in only at night when nobody is walking along the pontoon
why: 230 V, seawater and bare copper: no tape, no dry hands; the base has another cable.

fig.title: Shore cable
lines: Outer sheath cut, copper showing near the plug

q: The technician lifts the bunk and shows you the batteries. What do you do?
a: Ask him to show you the master switches and fit terminal covers; you do not touch the terminals
o: Check the terminals are tight with the winch handle while he watches
Note it and plan to buy terminal covers in town on Monday
Ask him to disconnect the bank so you can inspect each battery
why: A dropped spanner across the terminals is a fire; in a fire you must find the master switch in the dark.

fig.title: Battery compartment
lines: Under the aft bunk, terminals uncovered
Master switches: behind the companionway steps
Technician: "check they are tight if you like"

q: The technician asks how you plan to run the boat for the week. What is your plan?
a: Engine an hour morning and evening, fridge on, instruments and autopilot off when not needed
o: Run everything — 200 Ah will see the week out without charging
Keep the engine idling all night so the fridge never drains the bank
Fridge off, autopilot on all night — the autopilot matters more
why: About 100 Ah usable; a day's draw is near that, so charge twice a day and cut what is not in use.

fig.title: Power budget
lines: Fridge 5 A · instruments 2 A · lights 2 A · autopilot 4 A
